title: A wet shoe
dir: Quiet and close, as if telling someone something true and terrible. Slow. Let each short sentence land before the next.
paras: The only warning Herbert Riederer got... was a wet shoe.

He was twenty-four years old, a state conservation officer, standing on the breakwater at Montrose Harbor in Chicago. He'd just written a ticket to a man who was fishing without a license. The sun was out. The lake was flat.
Then he felt water coming over his foot.
He stepped up to higher ground. Behind him, he heard a rush. And when he turned around... the people who'd been standing on that pier were being washed into Lake Michigan.

Eight people drowned in Chicago that morning. There was no storm overhead. There was no earthquake. The National Weather Service still describes it as a killer wave that rose "under calm winds and a bright sunny sky."
It was a tsunami. On a lake.
And nobody in Chicago saw it coming, because the thing that caused it had left two hours earlier. It still happens on the Great Lakes more than a hundred times a year.

title: The lake that is not a lake
dir: Steady and a little warmer. You are painting a picture of a summer morning.
paras: Lake Michigan is called a lake. That's the first mistake.

It's three hundred and seven miles long, and more than a hundred miles wide. Stand on the shore in Chicago and there is no other side. There's only a horizon. Twelve million people live along its edge.

In Chicago, the lakefront is the city's front yard, and on a hot Saturday in June, it fills up. Swimmers on the beaches. Families on the grass. And out on the long concrete piers, the fishermen, because that's where the deep water is.
Saturday, June twenty-sixth, nineteen fifty-four, was going to be one of those days.

title: The storm that left
dir: Pick up the pace through the storm, then slow right down from "Then it was gone." Firm and direct on "Remember that."
paras: It began with a storm that was only passing through.

A line of squalls formed near La Crosse, Wisconsin, and ran southeast. Madison. Rockford. Milwaukee. At about half past seven in the morning, it crossed Chicago and blew out over the lake, moving at close to sixty miles an hour.
It was fast. It was violent. And it was brief. Along the lakefront, people got off the piers and waited it out.
Then it was gone. The sky cleared. The wind dropped. By the time the lifeguards came on duty, the lake was still.
So people did the most natural thing in the world. They went back.
Remember that. Everybody in this story did the sensible thing. They waited for the storm to pass. It passed. And two hours later... the lake came for them anyway.

title: North Avenue Beach
dir: Storytelling pace. Light, almost amused, on "they laughed". Drop the voice and slow down from "Seconds later". Say the last line flatly, with no drama.
paras: The first place it reached was North Avenue Beach.

Joseph Pecararo was the lifeguard captain there. He was twenty-four. When he arrived for work, the beach was almost empty. Two fishermen out on the hook-shaped pier. A line of rescue rowboats on the sand, in front of the beach house.
Then the lifeguards saw the water coming up toward the boats, and ran to pull them higher.
Pecararo remembered it like this. "And when we did... there was a wave."
A wall of water went straight over them and knocked them off their feet. And when they came up, they laughed. "We thought it was kind of funny," he said.
Seconds later, a man came running across the sand. A fisherman had been swept off the pier.
His name was John Jaworski. He'd gone fishing that morning with his son, Joseph, who was eighteen.
The lifeguards formed a line in the rough water, and found him. They were bringing his body to shore when a police car pulled up beside them, with four words.
"Dozens down at Montrose."

title: Montrose Harbor
dir: Slow and serious all the way through. Do not act it out; the facts carry it. A small pause before each person's name.
paras: Montrose Harbor is a few miles up the shore. Its breakwater was one of the best fishing spots in the city, and that morning, there were people all along it.
This is where Herbert Riederer was standing, with his ticket book, and his wet shoe.
The National Weather Service says the water at Montrose rose more than ten feet in a few minutes. Not a breaking wave, like at the ocean. A surge. The whole lake... lifting.

Riederer never forgot what he saw when he turned around. Decades later, he could still describe one woman. He said: "She was riding the crest of this huge wave into the harbor mouth... then she disappeared."
A husband and wife, Mae and Edward Gabriel, were among those later found drowned. She was forty-eight. He was forty-nine.
Divers pulled three bodies from the harbor that morning. Four more were found later.
One of them was Theodore Stempinski. He was the man Riederer had just ticketed. It seems that when the water came, he stopped to pick up his fishing gear.
The wave struck the shore all the way from the Chicago River, north to Wilmette.
And then, as quickly as it had come... it was gone. The lake went flat. The sun was still shining.

title: The wrong name
dir: Curious and a little brisker: the explaining begins here. Say the spelled letters slowly. Pause before the last word and say it clearly.
paras: In nineteen fifty-four, nobody called it a tsunami.
There'd been no earthquake. No wind to speak of. A wall of water had come out of a calm lake, under a clear sky, killed eight people, and left. It needed a name.
The experts had one ready. Saysh. It's spelled S, E, I, C, H, E.
A saysh is a slosh. Wind pushes the water of a lake toward one end. When the wind lets go, the water rocks back, like water in a bathtub.
It was the best explanation anyone had. For decades, that's what the disaster was called. The Chicago saysh.
But a saysh is slow. The whole lake tilts and rocks, over hours. This had been one violent surge, over in minutes.
When scientists went back to the nineteen fifty-four records with modern computer models, they found it had been a tsunami after all. A kind most people have never heard of.
Meteo-tsunami.

title: What a meteotsunami is
dir: Clear and patient, like explaining to a friend. Slightly brighter. Slow down on the last line.
paras: You know what a tsunami is. The sea floor moves, usually in an earthquake. It shoves the water above it, and a wave races outward.
A meteo-tsunami is the same kind of wave. The only difference is what does the shoving. Meteo... as in meteorology. It's a tsunami made by weather.
Here's how weather does it.

A fast line of storms carries a sudden jump in air pressure. In nineteen fifty-four, that jump crossed the lake at around sixty miles an hour. As it moves, it presses down on the water, and a small wave forms underneath it. A few inches high. Harmless.
But a wave in water travels at a speed that depends on how deep the water is. And this is the key to everything.

If the storm above is moving at the same speed as the wave below, it stays right on top of it, and it keeps pushing. It's like pushing a child on a swing at exactly the right moment. Every push adds to the last one.

Scientists at Noah call it a Goldilocks event. If the storm is too slow, nothing builds. If it's too fast, it leaves its wave behind. But a storm moving at just the right speed for that lake builds a wave that keeps growing, all the way across.
Then the wave reaches the shallows. It slows down. It piles up. A harbor squeezes it higher still.
A few inches, in the middle of the lake... becomes ten feet at the end of a pier.

title: Why it came in sunshine
dir: This is the reveal. Steady and deliberate, with a short pause after each time on the clock. Lower and slower for the last paragraph.
paras: That explains the size. It doesn't explain the strangest part. Why did it hit Chicago in sunshine, two hours after the storm?
Follow the clock.
Seven thirty. The storm crosses Chicago and heads out over the lake, toward the southeast. The wave is forming beneath it. But it's moving away from Chicago.
Ten past eight. Storm and wave arrive together at Michigan City, Indiana, about forty miles across the water. A five-foot wall of water goes over the breakwater.
And here's the cruel part. The fishermen in Michigan City had already run. They'd seen the squall coming, and gone for higher ground. The storm that made the wave was also their warning.
Then the wave hit the shore. And it bounced.
It turned around, and went back the way it had come. Forty miles of open lake, under a sky that was now clear. It took an hour and twenty minutes.
Nine thirty. It reaches Chicago.
The people on the piers were looking at a calm lake. The storm was long gone. What was about to reach them had been made by that storm... carried across the lake... and sent back.

title: Ten days later
dir: A change of mood: hopeful but restrained. Let "Nobody was hurt." stand on its own.
paras: What happened next is the part almost nobody knows.
Ten days later... it happened again.

On July sixth, nineteen fifty-four, a similar storm crossed Chicago. But this time, the city knew what a storm like that could leave behind. The weather service put out a warning. The beaches were cleared.

And the wave came. Water rushed into the parking lot at Loyola Beach. It ran up the steps of the beach house at North Avenue, the same beach where the lifeguards had laughed ten days before. Then it raced back out.
Nobody was hurt.
Two waves, ten days apart, on the same stretch of shore. Eight dead the first time. None the second. The only difference was that somebody told people to get away from the water.
And Chicago did one more thing. It fixed steel posts and cables along its breakwaters. Something to hold on to... the next time the lake rose.

title: Not a freak
dir: Brisker and building. Each date starts a new short story, so pause briefly after it. Slow, firm and quiet for the last line.
paras: For years, nineteen fifty-four was filed away as a freak. A once-in-a-lifetime accident.
It was not.

In twenty sixteen, scientists searched years of water-level records from all around the Great Lakes. They found that meteo-tsunamis big enough to be dangerous, a foot high or more, happen on average one hundred and six times a year. Lake Michigan gets the most.
Most are small, and most arrive when nobody is in the water. Not all of them.
July fourth, nineteen twenty-nine. Grand Haven, Michigan. A morning thunderstorm, then a wave that swept people off the pier. Ten were reported killed.

July fourth, two thousand three. Warren Dunes, Michigan. A storm passes. The sun comes out. Families go back into the water. Seven swimmers drown. Scientists later concluded the most likely cause. A meteo-tsunami only about a foot high, and the rip currents it set off, which kept pulling long after the wave was gone.

April, twenty eighteen. Ludington, Michigan. Water comes over the harbor walls, and damages docks and homes along the shore. It was April, so almost nobody was there. But this time, people took pictures, and Noah used them to recreate a Great Lakes meteo-tsunami in a computer for the first time.

June, twenty twenty-five. Lake Superior. A storm sets off a meteo-tsunami and a saysh at once. People film their beaches draining, until the lake bed lies bare. Then the water comes back. One gauge records a forty-five inch rise, the largest in its thirty years of records.
Look at the deadly ones. Nineteen twenty-nine. Nineteen fifty-four. Two thousand three. Every one came the same way. A storm. Then sunshine. Then the water.

title: Can anyone see the next one coming?
dir: Direct and practical, as if speaking to one person. Slow and firm on the last two sentences.
paras: So can anyone see the next one coming?
Not yet.

After Ludington, Noah placed a tsunami buoy in the middle of Lake Michigan, based on the ones that watch for tsunamis in the Pacific. It's anchored to the lake floor, and it listens for exactly this kind of wave. Scientists hope it will one day let them warn the shore in time.
But today, there's still no meteo-tsunami warning system for the Great Lakes.

So the warning has to be the one given by a scientist at Noah. In his words: "Most people are used to thinking that once the sun comes out, the dangers of a storm have passed. However, these meteo-tsunami waves can be deadly and destructive, and continue to impact the lakes for hours after the rain and thunder have stopped."

If you're ever on one of the Great Lakes, and a fast line of storms goes through, remember that. When the sun comes back, don't go straight back onto the pier. Don't go straight back into the water. Give the lake time.
And if you see the water suddenly rising, or suddenly pulling away from the shore... don't go and look. Go up.

title: The warning
dir: Quiet and reflective at first. Warmer and more personal on the share line. Lift the energy a little for the last two paragraphs.
paras: On June twenty-sixth, nineteen fifty-four, nobody on those piers was careless. They waited for the storm to pass. They went back when the sky was blue. Everything they could see told them it was over.
Herbert Riederer's only warning was a wet shoe. Most of the people around him didn't even get that.

Twelve million people live on the shores of this lake, and most of them have never heard the word meteo-tsunami. If you know someone who swims in it, fishes in it, or walks its piers... send them this.

And there's something else hidden in this region, that most of the people living right on top of it have never seen. It's twelve hundred feet under Detroit. It's the size of a city. And trucks are driving through it right now.
That's the next video. Subscribe, and I'll see you down there.
